issues.legal_issue: A statutory declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive against a challenge to the purpose unless the declaration resulted from a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared that the land was needed for a public purpose for a limestone quarry.
The appellant alleged that limestone was used to manufacture cement sold for profit, but did not establish that the government’s action was a colourable exercise of power.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the public-purpose declaration failed because the declaration was conclusive and no colourable exercise of power was shown; the Court expressed no concluded opinion on whether commercial cement production itself was a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, a declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive evidence of that purpose. It may nevertheless be challenged for colourable exercise of power. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. The State of Punjab.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and public_purpose_declaration_made and not colorable_exercise_shown

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A person brought a writ challenge to an acquisition of land.
predicates.public_purpose_declaration_made: The government formally declared that the land was needed for a public purpose.
predicates.colorable_exercise_shown: The challenger established that the government invoked its acquisition power for a private purpose or no genuine purpose.

issues.definition: When a writ challenge contests the public purpose of an acquisition, a formal public-purpose declaration is conclusive if the challenger has not established a colourable exercise of power.

issues.legal_issue: Emergency possession powers limited to waste or arable land cannot be exercised over forest land that is neither mainly used for cultivation nor barren.
material_facts: The government invoked emergency powers to take possession before an award and to dispense with the hearing of objections.
The acquired land contained about one hundred thousand trees, including numerous forest species.
The land was not mainly used for ploughing or raising crops, and its vegetation meant that it was not barren waste land.
issues.conclusion: The land was neither waste nor arable land within the meaning of the emergency-possession provision, so the government lacked authority to direct possession under that provision; the direction and the resulting acquisition proceedings were invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act permits urgent possession before an award only of waste or arable land. In this context, arable land means land mainly used for ploughing and raising crops, while waste land means land unfit for cultivation or habitation and desolate and barren, with little or no vegetation. Where jurisdiction depends on a preliminary finding of fact, a court reviewing the action may independently determine whether that finding is correct. The Court relied on R. v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White and Collins v. Minister of Health.

rule.if: land_acquisition_emergency_possession_proceeding and land_is_forest and not land_mainly_used_for_crops and not land_barren_with_little_vegetation

predicates.land_acquisition_emergency_possession_pr: The government invoked an emergency procedure to take possession of land before an award in an acquisition proceeding.
predicates.land_is_forest: The land contains substantial forest growth, including numerous trees.
predicates.land_mainly_used_for_crops: The land is mainly used for ploughing and raising crops.
predicates.land_barren_with_little_vegetation: The land is desolate and barren and has little or no vegetation.

issues.definition: In an emergency-possession proceeding, the direction is unauthorized when the land is forest, is not mainly used for crops, and is not barren with little vegetation.

issues.legal_issue: A government cannot dispense with a landholder’s right to object by relying on an emergency opinion that the land qualifies for emergency powers when the land does not meet the required description.
material_facts: The government formed an opinion that the emergency provision applied and directed that objections need not be heard.
The land was forest land and was neither waste nor arable land.
Dispensing with the objection procedure deprived the appellant of the opportunity to object to the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The government’s direction dispensing with objections was ultra vires; the related acquisition declaration and subsequent proceedings were also invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act permits the government to direct that the section 5A objection procedure does not apply where it considers the emergency provisions applicable. Although that opinion is ordinarily subjective, it may be challenged where the authority did not apply its mind or acted mala fide; the absence of grounds supporting the opinion may permit an inference that it was not honestly formed or that relevant facts were not considered. The Court relied on King Emperor v. Shibnath Banerjee, Jaichand Lal Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Estate and Trust Agencies Ltd. v. Singapore Improvement Trust, Ross Clunis v. Papadopovllos, and R. v. Australian Stevedoring Industry Board.

predicates.land_acquisition_emergency_exemption_pro: The government used an emergency procedure in an acquisition proceeding to dispense with the ordinary objection process.
predicates.land_not_waste_or_arable: The land did not qualify as either waste land or arable land for the emergency procedure.
predicates.objection_hearing_excluded: The government directed that affected persons would not receive the ordinary opportunity to object to the acquisition.

issues.definition: In an emergency-exemption proceeding, excluding the objection hearing is ultra vires when the land does not qualify for the emergency procedure.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of land that includes the estate and everything appertaining to it carries the underlying mineral rights unless those rights were expressly or impliedly reserved.
material_facts: Historical grants gave the holder the estate and described everything appertaining to it as belonging to him, without reserving mineral rights to the government.
The permanent settlement recognized estate holders as proprietors of the soil.
Historical records and subordinate leases were consistent with the holder exercising mineral rights, and the government had not asserted a reservation of those rights.
issues.conclusion: The appellant owned the minerals and sub-soil rights in the area, and the High Court’s contrary conclusion was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: A grant of the land or its surface ordinarily includes minerals beneath it unless the grant contains an express or implied reservation. The Court relied on Regulation VIII of 1793, Regulations I and II of 1793, Benares Regulation I of 1795, Ranjit Singh v. Kali Dasi Debi, Hari Narayan Singh v. Sriram Chakravarti, Durga Prasad Singh v. Braja Nath Bose, Sashi Bhushan Misra v. Jyoti Prasad Singh Deo, and Mitchell v. Mosley. It also held that the Mirzapur Stone Mahal Act did not remove the proprietor’s rights to sub-soil minerals.

predicates.mineral_title_dispute: A dispute arose over whether a holder of a land grant owned the minerals beneath the land.
predicates.land_grant_includes_estate_and_appurtena: The grant conveyed the land or estate together with what appertained to it.
predicates.no_mineral_reservation: The grant contained no express or implied reservation of mineral rights to the grantor.

issues.definition: In a mineral-title dispute, a grantee owns the underlying mineral rights when the grant includes the estate and its appurtenances and reserves no minerals.

issues.legal_issue: A former landholder is not entitled to restoration of possession when the relevant intermediary interest has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
material_facts: The appellant sought restoration of possession of the acquired land.
In a companion decision, the Court held that the appellant’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
issues.conclusion: The claim for restoration of possession was rejected because the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, as amended, and its conclusion in the companion decision, The State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, that the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state.

predicates.writ_proceeding_seeking_restoration: A former holder sought restoration of possession in a writ proceeding.
predicates.intermediary_interest_validly_vested_in_: The holder’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform law.

issues.definition: A request for restoration of possession is denied when the proceeding seeks restoration and the claimant’s intermediary interest has validly vested in the state.
